option_rationales.B: Tenderness may occur with reactive nodes but is nonspecific.
option_rationales.C: Fixation increases concern, but definitive diagnosis requires further evaluation.
option_rationales.D: A bruit is a finding and cannot independently establish a hormone disorder.
option_rationales.E: Many disorders do not produce palpable nodes.

questions.exam_strategy: Describe findings accurately and avoid diagnostic certainty from a single sign.

questions.stem: A patient with a history of lymph-node removal reports slowly increasing unilateral arm swelling. Which response best applies the assessment principles from the lymphatic unit?

options.text: Compare both limbs, characterize the swelling and skin, review the history, and arrange clinical follow-up.
Assume the swelling is an infection and apply heat without assessment.
Massage the area forcefully to move fluid back toward the chest.
Document the swelling as normal because lymph-node surgery always causes it.

questions.correct_rationale: Prior lymphatic disruption can contribute to lymphedema, but unilateral swelling needs assessment for change, skin condition, infection signs, and other causes. Compare sides and arrange follow-up rather than assuming or applying forceful massage.

option_rationales.A: This evaluates the change and relevant context without presuming the cause.
option_rationales.B: Heat and an infection diagnosis are not justified without assessment.
option_rationales.C: Forceful massage is not appropriate and may cause harm.
option_rationales.D: A known risk factor does not make every new swelling normal or safe to ignore.

questions.exam_strategy: A relevant history guides assessment but does not replace evaluation of new swelling.

questions.stem: A patient reports gradually worsening hearing. Which additional question best helps identify relevant exposures and associated symptoms?

options.text: "Have you noticed tinnitus, dizziness, ear pain or drainage, noise exposure, or medicines associated with hearing changes?"
"You have an ear infection, don't you?"
"Do you have a family history of dental decay?"
"Does your hearing change when you swallow?"

questions.correct_rationale: A focused ear history includes onset and pattern of hearing change, associated tinnitus, vertigo, pain or drainage, noise exposure, medications, and relevant history. Open, neutral questions avoid assuming infection or age-related loss.

option_rationales.A: This gathers symptoms and exposures that can shape the ear assessment.
option_rationales.B: It is leading and assumes an infection without assessment.
option_rationales.C: Dental history does not directly characterize hearing change.
option_rationales.D: Swallowing is not the most useful first question for gradual hearing loss.

questions.exam_strategy: Explore the symptom, associated findings, and relevant environmental or medication exposures.

questions.stem: Which tympanic-membrane appearance is most consistent with a normal otoscopic finding?

options.text: Gray, translucent membrane with no bulging or perforation.
Opaque, markedly bulging membrane with loss of landmarks.
Visible hole with fluid drainage from the canal.
Bright red membrane in every healthy adult.

questions.correct_rationale: A normal tympanic membrane is generally gray and translucent with identifiable landmarks. Color alone must be interpreted with symptoms and the full otoscopic view; a bulging membrane or perforation is abnormal.

option_rationales.A: This describes the usual normal appearance in the slide.
option_rationales.B: Bulging and obscured landmarks can be abnormal and require clinical correlation.
option_rationales.C: A visible perforation and drainage are not normal findings.
option_rationales.D: A red membrane is not the expected normal appearance and may reflect several causes.

questions.exam_strategy: Combine membrane appearance with symptoms and the whole ear examination.

questions.stem: A patient who swims frequently reports ear-canal pain that worsens when the nurse gently moves the auricle or presses the tragus. Which finding is most consistent with this pattern?

options.text: External-canal inflammation, as can occur with otitis externa.
A normal response proving middle-ear disease.
Presbycusis.
A definite tympanic-membrane perforation.

questions.correct_rationale: Pain with manipulation of the auricle or tragus is associated with external-canal inflammation. It supports, but does not independently prove, otitis externa; otoscopy and the broader history are still needed.

option_rationales.A: The pain pattern and water exposure are compatible with otitis externa.
option_rationales.B: Tragus tenderness does not prove middle-ear disease.
option_rationales.C: Presbycusis is age-associated sensorineural hearing loss, not canal tenderness.
option_rationales.D: The finding does not establish a tympanic-membrane perforation.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the location and provocation of pain to focus the ear examination, not to skip otoscopy.

questions.stem: Which statements about Rinne and Weber screening are accurate? Select all that apply.

options.text: In a normal Rinne pattern, air conduction is heard longer or louder than bone conduction.
A Weber sound heard equally in both ears is described as not lateralized.
A single Weber result should be interpreted with symptoms and, when needed, a Rinne result.
A fixed two-second Rinne result proves normal hearing in every frequency.
Any Weber lateralization identifies sensorineural loss in the ear where it is heard.

questions.correct_rationale: Rinne compares air and bone conduction qualitatively; a normal pattern is air conduction greater than bone conduction. Weber is normally perceived at midline or equally, while lateralization must be interpreted with other findings and does not by itself identify loss type.

option_rationales.A: This is the usual normal Rinne relationship.
option_rationales.B: Equal perception is a non-lateralized Weber response.
option_rationales.C: Combined interpretation and clinical context improve screening interpretation.
option_rationales.D: A precise elapsed time is not a universal guarantee of normal hearing or every frequency.
option_rationales.E: Lateralization can occur with conductive or sensorineural loss, with different side relationships.

questions.exam_strategy: Interpret direction and conduction pattern together; do not use an isolated fixed-time rule.

questions.stem: A tuning fork is placed at the patient's midline, and the sound is louder in the right ear. On the right, bone conduction is heard longer than air conduction. Which interpretation best fits these combined screening findings?

options.text: A possible right conductive hearing loss that needs clinical correlation.
A definite left sensorineural loss proven without further testing.
Normal bilateral hearing in every frequency.
A finding of impaired equilibrium rather than hearing.

questions.correct_rationale: Weber lateralization toward the right combined with bone conduction greater than air conduction on the right is consistent with possible right conductive loss. Tuning-fork tests are screening maneuvers; formal hearing assessment may be needed.

option_rationales.A: The Weber and negative Rinne pattern on the same side supports possible conductive loss there.
option_rationales.B: The combined pattern does not prove left sensorineural loss.
option_rationales.C: The results are not the expected symmetric normal pattern.
option_rationales.D: These are hearing-conduction tests, not the Romberg balance assessment.

questions.exam_strategy: Combine the Weber side with the Rinne relationship on each side.

questions.stem: An older adult says, "I hear people talking, but I cannot understand them when the room is noisy." What is the best nursing response?

options.text: Assess the hearing change and communication needs; age-related high-frequency loss is possible but should not be assumed without evaluation.
Tell the patient that reduced hearing is inevitable and no assessment is needed.
Assume the patient is ignoring instructions.
Speak from another room so the patient learns to listen more carefully.

questions.correct_rationale: Presbycusis often affects high-frequency hearing and speech discrimination, especially in background noise, but age alone does not establish the cause. Assess onset, functional impact, exposures, medications, and communication preferences.

option_rationales.A: This recognizes a possible age-related pattern while preserving individualized assessment.
option_rationales.B: Hearing changes are not inevitable in a way that makes assessment unnecessary.
option_rationales.C: The communication difficulty should not be interpreted as nonadherence or inattention.
option_rationales.D: Speaking from another room worsens communication and does not assess hearing.

questions.exam_strategy: Adapt communication while assessing the cause and functional effect of hearing changes.

questions.stem: A patient reports dizziness and recently fell. The nurse is considering a Romberg test. What is the safest approach?

options.text: Explain the test, stand close enough to guard the patient, use a clear area, and stop if balance becomes unsafe.
Ask the patient to stand unsupported with eyes closed near the edge of the bed.
Perform the test while the patient is walking down a hallway.
Leave the room so the patient will respond naturally.

questions.correct_rationale: Romberg assesses balance and requires fall precautions, especially in a patient with dizziness or a recent fall. The nurse should guard the patient and stop if the test is unsafe; slight sway alone is not interpreted without the full response.

option_rationales.A: This protects the patient while allowing a controlled assessment.
option_rationales.B: An unsupported position at the bed edge creates an avoidable fall risk.
option_rationales.C: The test is not performed while walking, and the patient should be guarded.
option_rationales.D: Leaving the patient unattended is unsafe.

questions.exam_strategy: Do not perform a balance test without guarding a patient at risk of falling.

questions.stem: A patient routinely inserts cotton-tipped applicators into the ear canal to remove wax. Which teaching points are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Avoid inserting objects into the ear canal because they can injure the canal or tympanic membrane.
An applicator can push cerumen deeper and contribute to impaction.
Seek advice if there is pain, drainage, sudden hearing change, or a history of ear surgery before using removal products.
Insert the applicator as far as possible as long as it is cotton-tipped.
Use another person's prescription ear drops if wax does not come out.

questions.correct_rationale: Objects in the canal can cause trauma or push wax inward. Symptoms or a history that raises concern should be assessed before using cerumen products; shared or unprescribed ear drops are not appropriate.

option_rationales.A: Avoiding canal instrumentation reduces risk of trauma and perforation.
option_rationales.B: Cotton-tipped applicators can move cerumen deeper rather than remove it.
option_rationales.C: Pain, drainage, sudden change, and prior ear surgery warrant individualized guidance.
option_rationales.D: Cotton does not make deep insertion safe.
option_rationales.E: Prescription drops should not be shared or used without appropriate assessment.

questions.exam_strategy: Teach safe ear care and identify symptoms that need evaluation rather than self-treatment.

questions.stem: After a sudden sharp ear pain during a flight, a patient reports drainage and reduced hearing from that ear. The nurse sees a possible tympanic-membrane defect. Which response is most appropriate?

options.text: Document the symptoms and appearance, keep the ear from further water or instrumentation, and arrange clinical evaluation.
Irrigate the canal forcefully to see whether the membrane is intact.
Insert a cotton swab to assess the depth of the opening.
Instill any available ear drops before clarifying the injury.

questions.correct_rationale: Pain, drainage, reduced hearing, and a possible perforation require evaluation. Avoid irrigation, instrumentation, and unverified drops that may worsen injury or be unsafe with a nonintact membrane.

option_rationales.A: This protects the ear and ensures the suspected perforation is assessed.
option_rationales.B: Irrigation can introduce fluid through a perforation and cause harm.
option_rationales.C: Instrumenting the canal can worsen the injury.
option_rationales.D: Some drops are inappropriate when the tympanic membrane may be perforated.

questions.exam_strategy: When membrane integrity is uncertain, avoid canal irrigation or unprescribed drops.

questions.stem: A patient reports that one side of the nose is often blocked. Which technique best assesses nasal patency safely?

options.text: Inspect the external nose and septum, then ask the patient to breathe through one nostril at a time while the other is gently occluded.
Occlude both nostrils and ask the patient to breathe deeply through the nose.
Insert a cotton applicator deeply into the blocked nostril.
Diagnose a deviated septum from the patient's report alone.

questions.correct_rationale: Inspect symmetry and the septum, then compare airflow one side at a time without inserting instruments into the nose. A subjective blockage alone does not establish the cause.

option_rationales.A: This compares each nostril safely and directly assesses patency.
option_rationales.B: Occluding both nostrils prevents the requested patency assessment and is uncomfortable.
option_rationales.C: Deep insertion can injure mucosa and is not needed for this screening.
option_rationales.D: A deviated septum requires examination; symptoms alone are insufficient.

questions.exam_strategy: Compare each side separately and avoid unnecessary intranasal instrumentation.

questions.stem: A patient reports pressure over the cheeks and forehead, nasal congestion, and tenderness with gentle sinus palpation. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

options.text: The findings can occur with sinus inflammation, but history, duration, associated symptoms, and examination are needed to determine the cause.
Tenderness proves bacterial sinusitis and requires antibiotics.
The findings establish a nasal polyp.
Sinus tenderness is always a normal finding and needs no assessment.

questions.correct_rationale: Facial pressure, congestion, and tenderness may occur with sinus inflammation but are not specific for bacterial infection. The cause and need for treatment depend on the full history and clinical evaluation.

option_rationales.A: This connects the findings to a possible source without overdiagnosing.
option_rationales.B: Tenderness alone cannot determine bacterial cause or antibiotic need.
option_rationales.C: A nasal polyp is a separate finding that requires inspection.
option_rationales.D: New pain or tenderness should be interpreted with the patient's symptoms.

questions.exam_strategy: Treat a physical sign as evidence to interpret, not a standalone diagnosis.

questions.stem: A patient reports intermittent nasal obstruction and occasional nosebleeds. Which assessment steps are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Inspect the external nose for symmetry and skin changes.
Compare airflow through each nostril separately.
Ask about duration, triggers, allergies, trauma, medications, and bleeding pattern.
Insert a cotton swab deeply to check the nasal passage.
Press firmly over both sinuses until the patient reports pain.

questions.correct_rationale: External inspection, one-sided patency comparison, and a focused history help assess obstruction and epistaxis. Deep instrumentation and forceful sinus palpation are unnecessary and can injure the patient.

option_rationales.A: Inspection provides information about symmetry and visible abnormalities.
option_rationales.B: Testing each side separately identifies unilateral obstruction.
option_rationales.C: Triggers, trauma, medications, and timing provide context for symptoms and bleeding.
option_rationales.D: Deep cotton-swab insertion risks mucosal injury and is not a routine assessment technique.
option_rationales.E: Forceful pressure is painful and does not improve the assessment.

questions.exam_strategy: Gather a focused history and use gentle external techniques before considering further evaluation.

questions.stem: A patient develops a nosebleed while seated in the clinic. The patient is alert and has no signs of major blood loss. Which initial instruction is most appropriate?

options.text: Sit upright, lean slightly forward, and apply continuous pressure to the soft part of the nose.
Tilt the head far back and swallow the blood.
Lie flat and pack the nose deeply with tissue.
Blow the nose forcefully until the bleeding stops.

questions.correct_rationale: For an uncomplicated anterior nosebleed, sitting upright, leaning forward, and pinching the soft part continuously helps control bleeding while limiting swallowed blood. Persistent or severe bleeding requires escalation.

option_rationales.A: This position and pressure are appropriate initial measures for a stable patient.
option_rationales.B: Tilting backward encourages blood to run into the throat and be swallowed or aspirated.
option_rationales.C: Deep packing without training or an order risks trauma and is not the first step.
option_rationales.D: Forceful blowing can disrupt clot formation and worsen bleeding.

questions.exam_strategy: Use forward positioning and continuous soft-nose pressure; avoid directing blood into the throat.

questions.stem: A patient using an inhaled corticosteroid has white patches on the buccal mucosa and tongue with soreness. Which response is most appropriate?

options.text: Document the location and appearance, ask about inhaler and mouth-rinsing technique, and notify the clinician for evaluation.
Scrape the patches forcefully to confirm the diagnosis.
Tell the patient that every white oral patch is harmless food residue.
Stop all prescribed medication immediately without consulting the prescriber.

questions.correct_rationale: White oral patches and soreness can be consistent with candidiasis, which is associated with inhaled corticosteroid use, but assessment and clinical evaluation are needed. Mouth-rinsing technique and adherence to prescribed therapy can be reviewed without stopping medication independently.

option_rationales.A: This captures the finding and relevant exposure while arranging appropriate evaluation.
option_rationales.B: Forceful scraping can injure mucosa and is not needed to establish the nursing assessment.
option_rationales.C: Persistent patches with soreness should not be assumed to be food residue.
option_rationales.D: Abruptly stopping prescribed treatment without clinician guidance is unsafe.

questions.exam_strategy: Describe oral lesions and review relevant medication technique without making an independent diagnosis.

questions.stem: A patient with markedly enlarged tonsils is drooling, unable to swallow secretions, and making a high-pitched inspiratory sound. What is the priority?

options.text: Activate emergency assistance and prioritize airway evaluation.
Offer oral fluids and ask the patient to gargle.
Complete a detailed dental history before responding.
Document uncomplicated tonsillitis and schedule routine follow-up.

questions.correct_rationale: Drooling, inability to handle secretions, and inspiratory stridor suggest possible upper-airway compromise. Immediate airway escalation is more important than oral intake or a complete routine examination.

option_rationales.A: Stridor with impaired secretion handling is an airway emergency.
option_rationales.B: Oral fluids can increase aspiration risk when swallowing is impaired.
option_rationales.C: A detailed history must not delay emergency airway assessment.
option_rationales.D: This is not an uncomplicated outpatient presentation.

questions.exam_strategy: Prioritize stridor and secretion difficulty as potential airway compromise.

questions.stem: A nurse is completing an oral and throat assessment. Which actions or observations are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Inspect the lips, oral mucosa, gums, teeth, tongue, and visible throat.
Note color, lesions or white patches, odor, and the presence or absence of tonsils.
Ask about pain, swallowing difficulty, oral hygiene, and relevant dental or medication history.
Assume a white patch is candidiasis without recording its appearance or context.
Use a tongue blade despite severe stridor and inability to manage secretions.

questions.correct_rationale: A systematic inspection covers oral structures and describes visible findings; a focused history adds symptoms and risk context. A possible airway emergency takes priority over routine oral inspection.

option_rationales.A: These structures are part of a thorough oral and throat assessment.
option_rationales.B: These objective observations can identify abnormalities and guide follow-up.
option_rationales.C: Pain, dysphagia, hygiene, and medication history help interpret findings.
option_rationales.D: A white patch has multiple possible causes and must be assessed in context.
option_rationales.E: Instrumenting the throat in a patient with stridor may worsen airway risk and should not delay emergency response.

questions.exam_strategy: Inspect systematically, describe rather than diagnose, and prioritize airway stability.

questions.stem: During a meal, a patient coughs repeatedly after swallowing thin liquids and develops a wet-sounding voice. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Stop oral intake, assess breathing and swallowing safety, and promptly notify the appropriate clinician.
Offer a larger sip to determine whether the cough is reproducible.
Document normal swallowing because the patient can speak.
Place the patient supine and continue the meal.

questions.correct_rationale: Coughing with liquids and a wet voice can indicate impaired swallowing and aspiration risk. Stop the trial, ensure respiratory stability, and arrange further evaluation rather than continuing to challenge swallowing.

option_rationales.A: This reduces further aspiration exposure and initiates appropriate assessment.
option_rationales.B: A larger sip may increase aspiration risk and is not a safe test.
option_rationales.C: Ability to speak does not establish safe swallowing.
option_rationales.D: Supine positioning and continued intake increase risk.

questions.exam_strategy: Treat coughing and wet voice during swallowing as a safety signal, not a cue to keep testing orally.

questions.stem: A patient reports recurrent sore throat and intermittent hoarseness. Which focused-history questions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Ask about duration, progression, fever, pain, swallowing, and voice changes.
Ask about tobacco or irritant exposure, reflux symptoms, and relevant environmental exposures.
Ask whether there is difficulty breathing, drooling, or inability to swallow secretions.
Assume the cause is contagious without asking about symptoms or exposure.
Ask only about the patient's ancestry because that determines the cause.

questions.correct_rationale: A focused ENMT history explores symptom pattern, associated swallowing or airway symptoms, and relevant exposures. Breathing difficulty or inability to handle secretions changes urgency; ancestry alone does not determine the cause.

option_rationales.A: These details characterize the symptom and its progression.
option_rationales.B: Irritants and reflux can be relevant contributors to recurrent throat or voice symptoms.
option_rationales.C: Airway and secretion-handling symptoms are important red flags.
option_rationales.D: A presumed contagious cause is not a substitute for a focused assessment.
option_rationales.E: The slide's ancestry generalization is unsupported and is not an individualized clinical assessment.

questions.exam_strategy: Ask about symptoms, airway safety, and relevant exposures without stereotyping or presuming etiology.

questions.stem: A pregnant patient reports bilateral nasal stuffiness without fever, facial pain, or purulent drainage. Which response is most appropriate?

options.text: Acknowledge that pregnancy-related vascular changes can contribute, assess severity and associated symptoms, and avoid assuming infection.
Diagnose bacterial sinusitis based on congestion alone.
Tell the patient the symptom is imaginary because the external nose looks normal.
Recommend any decongestant without checking pregnancy-specific guidance.

questions.correct_rationale: Pregnancy-related vascular changes can contribute to nasal congestion, but the nurse should assess associated symptoms and severity. Congestion alone does not establish infection, and medication choices during pregnancy require individualized guidance.

option_rationales.A: This recognizes a possible developmental consideration without assuming cause or treatment.
option_rationales.B: Congestion alone does not diagnose bacterial sinusitis.
option_rationales.C: A normal external appearance does not invalidate the patient's symptom.
option_rationales.D: Medication choices in pregnancy should be checked with an appropriate clinician.

questions.exam_strategy: Use developmental context without dismissing symptoms or making an unsupported diagnosis.

questions.stem: Which statements about common ENMT assessment findings are accurate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Dysphagia means difficulty swallowing.
Presbycusis commonly affects high-frequency hearing and may impair speech understanding in noise.
Weber lateralization requires interpretation with the clinical context and other hearing findings.
A normal Romberg result proves normal hearing acuity.
Any white oral patch can be diagnosed as thrush from color alone.

questions.correct_rationale: Dysphagia describes difficulty swallowing; presbycusis can affect high-frequency hearing; and Weber lateralization is not diagnostic on its own. Romberg assesses balance, while oral patches require contextual assessment.

option_rationales.A: This is the definition of dysphagia.
option_rationales.B: High-frequency hearing loss can make speech harder to understand, especially with background noise.
option_rationales.C: Lateralization may reflect different hearing-loss patterns and needs correlation.
option_rationales.D: Romberg evaluates balance and does not establish hearing acuity.
option_rationales.E: White patches have multiple causes and require examination and history.

questions.exam_strategy: Know what each bedside test measures and avoid interpreting one sign in isolation.

questions.stem: A patient walks quickly into the clinic and has a respiratory rate of 24/min while speaking. The patient is not in distress. What is the best next step?

options.text: Allow the patient to rest, then reassess the rate, depth, pattern, and effort in context.
Document the rate as the patient's resting baseline.
Diagnose pneumonia based on the rate alone.
Ask the patient to breathe more slowly while counting the rate.

questions.correct_rationale: Recent exertion can temporarily raise respiratory rate. Reassess after rest and observe effort, depth, pattern, symptoms, and baseline rather than interpreting one post-activity count as a resting value or a diagnosis.

option_rationales.A: Rest and repeat assessment help determine whether the rate remains elevated and whether distress is present.
option_rationales.B: A post-exertion measurement is not a resting baseline.
option_rationales.C: Respiratory rate alone cannot diagnose pneumonia.
option_rationales.D: Coaching the patient to alter breathing can distort the measurement.

questions.exam_strategy: Measure under appropriate conditions and interpret the rate with effort and context.

questions.stem: Which observation is most important to include during the initial inspection of an adult's anterior and posterior thorax?

options.text: Symmetry, skin color, respiratory rate, depth, pattern, and visible work of breathing.
The patient's preferred sleep position only.
The presence of a cough, without observing breathing at rest.
The exact shape of the nose and the color of the iris.

questions.correct_rationale: Respiratory inspection begins with the thorax and breathing: symmetry, configuration, rate, depth, pattern, skin color, and effort. History adds important context but does not replace direct observation.

option_rationales.A: These observations directly characterize respiratory status at the time of assessment.
option_rationales.B: Sleep position may be relevant history but is not a complete thoracic inspection.
option_rationales.C: A cough history alone does not assess current respiratory effort or pattern.
option_rationales.D: These features do not assess the respiratory system.

questions.exam_strategy: Start with a structured look at how the patient is breathing now.

questions.stem: While auscultating a healthy adult, the nurse hears loud, high-pitched bronchial sounds over a peripheral lung field. How should this finding be interpreted?

options.text: It is unexpected in a peripheral field and should be reassessed and interpreted with other findings.
It is expected because bronchial sounds are loudest over all lung tissue.
It proves the patient has asthma.
It means the stethoscope should be placed over clothing.

questions.correct_rationale: Bronchial breath sounds are normally heard over the trachea; vesicular sounds are expected over most peripheral lung fields. A peripheral bronchial quality is abnormal and can reflect altered sound transmission, but it is not diagnostic by itself.

option_rationales.A: This recognizes the location mismatch and calls for reassessment and correlation.
option_rationales.B: Bronchial sounds are not normally heard throughout peripheral fields.
option_rationales.C: Bronchial sound location does not diagnose asthma.
option_rationales.D: Auscultate directly on skin when possible; clothing can distort sounds.

questions.exam_strategy: Interpret breath-sound quality together with where it is heard.

questions.stem: Which actions support a systematic lung auscultation? Select all that apply.

options.text: Place the diaphragm on bare skin when possible.
Compare corresponding areas side to side in a consistent sequence.
Listen through a full respiratory cycle at each site when feasible.
Ask the patient to breathe deeply through the mouth and pause if dizzy.
Listen to only one posterior site and infer the rest of the lung fields.

questions.correct_rationale: Auscultating on skin, comparing paired fields, and listening through inspiration and expiration support a reliable assessment. Deep breathing can cause dizziness, so pause as needed; one site cannot represent both lungs.

option_rationales.A: Clothing can create friction sounds or obscure breath sounds.
option_rationales.B: Side-to-side comparison helps identify asymmetry.
option_rationales.C: A full respiratory cycle allows the nurse to compare inspiratory and expiratory sounds.
option_rationales.D: Mouth breathing can improve sound assessment, and stopping for dizziness protects the patient.
option_rationales.E: A single site is insufficient to assess the distribution of sounds.

questions.exam_strategy: Use a consistent ladder pattern and compare matching areas on both sides.

questions.stem: A patient reports a persistent cough. Which follow-up question yields the most useful focused assessment information?

options.text: "When does it occur, is it dry or productive, what does the sputum look and smell like, and is there pain or blood?"
"You probably have an allergy, correct?"
"Can you stop coughing while I finish the exam?"
"Do you want me to document pneumonia?"

questions.correct_rationale: Cough assessment includes timing, quality, productivity, sputum characteristics, associated pain, blood, exposures, and impact. An open symptom question gathers information without presuming the cause.

option_rationales.A: These details characterize the cough and identify findings that may change urgency.
option_rationales.B: It assumes an allergic cause before assessment.
option_rationales.C: It discourages reporting and does not assess the symptom.
option_rationales.D: The nurse should not diagnose pneumonia from the patient's report alone.

questions.exam_strategy: Describe cough and sputum before inferring an etiology.

questions.stem: A patient develops a harsh, high-pitched sound during inspiration with suprasternal retractions and difficulty speaking. What is the priority response?

options.text: Activate emergency assistance and prioritize airway assessment.
Continue a routine posterior percussion sequence.
Ask the patient to cough forcefully and reassess in an hour.
Document this as a normal vesicular sound.

questions.correct_rationale: Inspiratory stridor with retractions and difficulty speaking suggests upper-airway obstruction and potential rapid deterioration. Emergency airway response takes priority over completing a routine respiratory examination.

option_rationales.A: The findings indicate immediate airway risk.
option_rationales.B: Percussion is not the priority in a patient with signs of upper-airway compromise.
option_rationales.C: Waiting or provoking a cough could delay necessary intervention.
option_rationales.D: Stridor is not a normal vesicular breath sound.

questions.exam_strategy: Recognize upper-airway noise and increased work of breathing as urgent.

questions.stem: Which findings indicate increased respiratory distress and require prompt reassessment or escalation? Select all that apply.

options.text: New accessory-muscle use and suprasternal retractions.
Inability to speak a full sentence because of breathlessness.
New cyanosis or decreasing level of alertness.
Markedly reduced air movement in a patient who is tiring.
A comfortable patient with an even pattern and no increased effort.

questions.correct_rationale: Retractions, inability to speak comfortably, cyanosis, altered alertness, and poor air movement with fatigue are concerning signs of respiratory compromise. A comfortable, even pattern without effort is reassuring but should still be interpreted with the patient's baseline.

option_rationales.A: Accessory-muscle use and retractions signal increased work of breathing.
option_rationales.B: Speech limited by breathlessness can reflect significant respiratory distress.
option_rationales.C: Cyanosis or declining alertness can indicate hypoxemia or deterioration.
option_rationales.D: A tiring patient with very little air movement may be critically ill even if wheezing decreases.
option_rationales.E: This describes a relatively reassuring pattern without the listed distress signs.

questions.exam_strategy: Assess effort, speech, color, alertness, and air movement—not rate alone.

questions.stem: The nurse finds increased tactile fremitus over one area of the posterior lung and hears bronchial-quality sounds in that same peripheral region. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

options.text: The findings may reflect increased sound transmission through consolidated lung and require correlation with the full examination.
The findings prove a pneumothorax.
Increased fremitus is expected over a large pleural effusion.
The findings are normal because bronchial sounds are expected over all posterior fields.

questions.correct_rationale: Consolidated lung can transmit voice vibrations and breath sounds more strongly, producing increased fremitus and bronchial-quality sounds in an abnormal location. These findings support further assessment but are not diagnostic alone.

option_rationales.A: The paired findings are compatible with consolidation and need clinical correlation.
option_rationales.B: Pneumothorax typically reduces or abolishes breath sounds and fremitus on the affected side.
option_rationales.C: Pleural fluid usually dampens tactile fremitus over the affected region.
option_rationales.D: Bronchial sounds are normally heard over the trachea, not throughout posterior peripheral fields.

questions.exam_strategy: Interpret sound and vibration findings together and by location.

questions.stem: Percussion over the right lower posterior thorax is dull, with decreased breath sounds and decreased tactile fremitus in the same region. Which condition is most consistent with this combination?

options.text: Pleural effusion, which can dampen sound transmission over the fluid.
A normal air-filled lung in every case.
An uncomplicated small airway wheeze.
A tension pneumothorax established by these findings alone.

questions.correct_rationale: Pleural fluid can produce dullness to percussion and reduce breath sounds and tactile fremitus over the affected area. The pattern suggests an abnormality but still requires evaluation with symptoms and other findings.

option_rationales.A: The combined findings are compatible with fluid in the pleural space.
option_rationales.B: Dullness with reduced sounds and fremitus is not the expected normal air-filled-lung pattern.
option_rationales.C: Wheeze is an auscultatory airway sound and does not explain this percussion/fremitus pattern.
option_rationales.D: These findings alone do not establish tension physiology or a specific emergency diagnosis.

questions.exam_strategy: Use percussion, breath sounds, and fremitus as a pattern rather than relying on one sign.

questions.stem: Which statements about respiratory assessment findings are accurate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Wheezes can occur with narrowed airways, but do not by themselves prove asthma.
Crackles may occur with fluid or reopening of small airways and need clinical correlation.
Decreased fremitus can occur over pleural effusion or pneumothorax.
Increased fremitus can occur over consolidated lung.
Auscultation findings alone identify the exact cause of every respiratory disorder.

questions.correct_rationale: Wheezes, crackles, and changes in fremitus provide useful but nonspecific clues. Their location, symmetry, timing, associated symptoms, and other assessment findings determine their significance.

option_rationales.A: Wheezing indicates narrowed airways but can have more than one cause.
option_rationales.B: Crackles have several mechanisms and should be interpreted in context.
option_rationales.C: Pleural air or fluid can reduce vibration transmission to the chest wall.
option_rationales.D: Consolidation can transmit vocal vibrations more strongly.
option_rationales.E: No single auscultation finding identifies every cause with certainty.

questions.exam_strategy: Treat breath sounds as clues that must be integrated with the rest of the examination.

questions.stem: A patient reports needing three pillows to sleep because breathing worsens when lying flat. The nurse also hears bilateral crackles and observes new ankle edema. What is the best response?

options.text: Keep the patient in the position that eases breathing, assess oxygenation and vital signs, and promptly notify the clinician.
Place the patient flat to see whether the symptoms can be reproduced.
Document the findings as normal aging and continue routine care.
Conclude that pneumonia is the only possible cause.

questions.correct_rationale: Orthopnea with crackles and new edema can indicate fluid overload or heart failure and warrants prompt assessment. Support breathing in the patient's preferred upright position and communicate the combined findings without making a definitive diagnosis.

option_rationales.A: This supports breathing while assessing and escalating a concerning cardiopulmonary pattern.
option_rationales.B: Provoking dyspnea is unsafe and unnecessary.
option_rationales.C: New orthopnea, crackles, and edema are not findings to normalize as aging.
option_rationales.D: Several conditions can produce crackles; the full pattern needs clinical evaluation.

questions.exam_strategy: Combine orthopnea, crackles, and edema and avoid deliberately worsening breathing.

questions.concept: Severe asthma and reduced air movement
questions.stem: A patient with a history of asthma initially has loud wheezing. The patient becomes drowsy, appears exhausted, and now has very little audible air movement. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Treat the change as impending respiratory failure and activate emergency assistance.
Reassure the patient that less wheezing means the asthma is resolving.
Wait for the next scheduled assessment because the patient is no longer coughing.
Ask the patient to walk to improve lung expansion.

questions.correct_rationale: A tiring or drowsy patient with minimal air movement may have critically severe obstruction; disappearance of wheeze can reflect inadequate airflow rather than improvement. Immediate emergency response is required.

option_rationales.A: The decline in alertness and air movement indicates possible impending respiratory failure.
option_rationales.B: Reduced wheezing with poor air movement is not reassuring.
option_rationales.C: Waiting can delay lifesaving intervention.
option_rationales.D: Exertion is unsafe in a deteriorating patient.

questions.exam_strategy: Listen for air movement and assess fatigue; a quieter chest can be more dangerous than loud wheezing.

questions.stem: A patient with asthma wants to identify patterns that worsen symptoms. Which exposures or activities can be asthma triggers for some people? Select all that apply.

options.text: Allergens such as pollen or dust mites.
Respiratory infections.
Exercise, especially with cold dry air for some patients.
Tobacco smoke or other airway irritants.
Every patient with asthma has the same trigger, so individual history is unnecessary.

questions.correct_rationale: Asthma triggers vary and can include allergens, respiratory infections, exercise, cold air, smoke, and other irritants. A focused history identifies the individual patient's pattern; allergens are not the only possible trigger.

option_rationales.A: Pollen and dust mites can trigger symptoms in some patients.
option_rationales.B: Respiratory infections can worsen asthma symptoms.
option_rationales.C: Exercise and cold, dry air can trigger bronchoconstriction for some people.
option_rationales.D: Smoke and irritants can provoke airway symptoms.
option_rationales.E: Triggers differ among patients and should be assessed individually.

questions.exam_strategy: Ask the patient about their own trigger pattern rather than assuming asthma is always allergic.

questions.stem: On the first day after abdominal surgery, a patient has shallow breathing, reduced movement, and diminished breath sounds at both bases. Which response is most appropriate?

options.text: Assess oxygenation, pain, mobility, and the prescribed pulmonary-care plan; report worsening findings and support ordered breathing/mobility measures.
Assume this is harmless because reduced breath sounds are expected after surgery.
Diagnose pneumonia and request antibiotics without further evaluation.
Keep the patient immobile to prevent discomfort.

questions.correct_rationale: Postoperative shallow breathing and immobility increase atelectasis risk, but diminished sounds require assessment of oxygenation, pain, and the full clinical picture. Support prescribed pulmonary hygiene and mobility measures and communicate deterioration.

option_rationales.A: This addresses likely contributors while monitoring for worsening or alternative causes.
option_rationales.B: Postoperative status does not make new abnormal findings harmless.
option_rationales.C: The findings do not establish pneumonia or justify independent antibiotic treatment.
option_rationales.D: Immobility can worsen pulmonary complications.

questions.exam_strategy: Connect postoperative immobility with atelectasis risk but assess before assigning a diagnosis.

questions.stem: A patient has progressive dyspnea and a unilateral area of dullness with reduced breath sounds and fremitus. Imaging later identifies pleural fluid. Which statement about the assessment is most accurate?

options.text: The physical findings are compatible with pleural effusion; drainage decisions and thoracentesis are performed by qualified clinicians.
Increased fremitus over the fluid is the expected finding in every effusion.
The nurse should insert a needle to remove the fluid at the bedside.
Dullness alone proves the fluid is infected.

questions.correct_rationale: Pleural effusion can produce dullness and decreased breath sounds and fremitus. The assessment supports the diagnosis in context, but does not determine etiology; thoracentesis is a procedure performed by an appropriately qualified clinician.

option_rationales.A: This appropriately links the findings with effusion and respects procedural scope.
option_rationales.B: Pleural fluid usually decreases transmission of fremitus over the affected area.
option_rationales.C: Thoracentesis is not a routine nursing procedure and requires qualified procedural care.
option_rationales.D: Dullness cannot identify infection on its own.

questions.exam_strategy: Recognize the effusion pattern and distinguish assessment from invasive treatment.

questions.stem: A patient suddenly develops unilateral pleuritic chest pain and severe dyspnea. Which findings or actions support urgent evaluation for possible pneumothorax? Select all that apply.

options.text: Unilateral markedly diminished or absent breath sounds.
Acute worsening oxygenation or hemodynamic instability.
Rapid emergency escalation while supporting airway and breathing.
A new asymmetry in chest expansion.
Waiting to finish the routine auscultation sequence before seeking help.

questions.correct_rationale: Sudden unilateral pain and dyspnea with asymmetric expansion or absent breath sounds can indicate pneumothorax; instability raises urgency further. Escalate promptly and support airway and breathing rather than delaying for a complete exam.

option_rationales.A: Absent or markedly decreased unilateral sounds are concerning in this acute context.
option_rationales.B: Worsening oxygenation or instability may indicate life-threatening progression.
option_rationales.C: Immediate escalation is appropriate for acute respiratory deterioration.
option_rationales.D: Asymmetric expansion supports the need for urgent evaluation.
option_rationales.E: Completing a routine sequence must not delay emergency response.

questions.exam_strategy: Sudden unilateral respiratory change plus instability takes priority over completing the exam.

questions.stem: A patient reports coughing up bright-red blood and is now short of breath. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Assess airway, breathing, oxygenation, and the amount of bleeding while initiating urgent clinical escalation.
Ask the patient to lie flat and continue the interview.
Reassure the patient that blood in sputum is always from dry air.
Delay assessment until the patient can provide a full environmental history.

questions.correct_rationale: Hemoptysis with dyspnea can threaten airway and breathing and requires immediate assessment and escalation. A focused history is useful after stabilizing the immediate respiratory concern.

option_rationales.A: Airway, breathing, oxygenation, and bleeding severity determine immediate safety needs.
option_rationales.B: A flat position may worsen breathing and does not prioritize safety.
option_rationales.C: Hemoptysis has multiple potential causes and should not be dismissed.
option_rationales.D: A complete exposure history must not delay urgent respiratory assessment.

questions.exam_strategy: When blood and breathing difficulty occur together, assess airway and breathing before routine history.

questions.stem: An adult's anterior-posterior chest diameter appears nearly equal to the transverse diameter. The patient has a long smoking history and prolonged expiration. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: The increased AP diameter can occur with chronic hyperinflation, but the nurse should correlate it with symptoms and other findings.
A 1:1 chest ratio is the expected finding in every healthy adult.
The chest shape alone proves emphysema.
The finding is a pectus excavatum deformity.

questions.correct_rationale: An adult AP-to-transverse ratio near 1:1 can occur with chronic hyperinflation, including emphysema, but it is not diagnostic by itself. The normal adult ratio is generally closer to 1:2, and the full respiratory history and examination matter.

option_rationales.A: This identifies a possible chronic pattern without treating appearance as a diagnosis.
option_rationales.B: A near 1:1 ratio is not the usual adult chest configuration.
option_rationales.C: Chest shape alone cannot prove emphysema.
option_rationales.D: Pectus excavatum describes a depressed sternum, not generalized AP enlargement.

questions.exam_strategy: Interpret chest configuration with history, effort, and auscultation rather than diagnosing from shape alone.

questions.stem: Which statements about respiratory-rate interpretation are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: For a resting adult, 12–20 breaths/minute is a common reference range, but symptoms and baseline also matter.
A persistent rate of 25/minute in a resting adult should be assessed rather than automatically normalized as aging.
Infant and child rates must be interpreted using age-specific references and the child's state.
Rate should be interpreted with depth, pattern, effort, oxygenation, and clinical context.
A single rate can diagnose the cause of respiratory distress.

questions.correct_rationale: Adult respiratory rate is commonly referenced at 12–20/minute at rest, but the patient's baseline, effort, symptoms, and context matter. Pediatric rates vary with age and state, and no single rate diagnoses an etiology.

option_rationales.A: This is a common resting adult reference range, interpreted alongside other findings.
option_rationales.B: A persistent rate above the common adult range needs assessment, not automatic age-based reassurance.
option_rationales.C: Pediatric respiratory rates vary by age and state.
option_rationales.D: Rate alone omits important indicators of work and gas exchange.
option_rationales.E: Rate is a finding, not a stand-alone diagnosis.

questions.exam_strategy: Interpret age-appropriate rate together with respiratory effort, symptoms, and the broader assessment.

questions.stem: A mechanically ventilated patient develops fever, purulent respiratory secretions, new crackles, and increased oxygen needs. Which interpretation is most accurate?

options.text: The patient needs prompt evaluation for possible ventilator-associated pneumonia; ventilation increases risk but is not itself an infectious cause.
Mechanical ventilation alone proves pneumonia and identifies the organism.
The findings are expected during ventilation and need no assessment.
Crackles exclude pneumonia because pneumonia causes only wheezing.

questions.correct_rationale: Fever, secretions, new lung findings, and increased oxygen need warrant evaluation for ventilator-associated pneumonia and other complications. Mechanical ventilation increases risk by impairing airway defenses but does not itself identify an infectious cause or pathogen.

option_rationales.A: This recognizes a concerning change and correctly distinguishes risk from etiology.
option_rationales.B: Ventilation is a risk factor, not proof of infection or its organism.
option_rationales.C: New fever, secretions, crackles, and oxygen needs are not findings to dismiss.
option_rationales.D: Pneumonia can cause crackles; wheezing is not required.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the whole change from baseline and distinguish a risk factor from the cause of infection.
